# Coffee Bean Prices Fall. Are Price Tags Still on a Journey?

“Beans cost less now!” When you hear that, your wallet pumps its fist. You already imagine your usual cup costing less, too. But a shop’s price may not change right away. When a price tag makes you ask, “Haven’t you heard the news?”, it feels like there is a delay.

The International Coffee Organization shared a measure of coffee prices. It fell 8.7% from the month before. The group said more beans picked in Brazil had reached the market. It also expected a good supply to continue.

The US Department of Agriculture said several things had raised prices at once. There was bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam. Fewer beans were for sale. Demand was also strong.

At the same time, US data on what people pay showed coffee cost 6.1% more than in the same month a year earlier. You might wonder, “Did prices fall or rise?” But this data was for a different month than the bean price measure. It also does not show the price of coffee at a cafe. Don’t put the two numbers in the ring just yet.

So, how long does it take for bean prices to reach a price tag?

People in the market and experts spoke with Reuters. They estimate raw-bean prices take at least about nine months to appear in US shop prices. The road to a price tag is quite a long journey.

The article says US companies that roast coffee keep raw beans in stock. Roasting and packing the beans also take time. These companies often talk with stores about prices on a regular basis. A shop’s price tag does not change the moment the market moves.

However, “about nine months” is an estimate based on interviews. It is not a rule for every company. And it is not a promise that “prices will fall in nine months.” It is too soon to mark the date on your calendar.

A cafe cup also costs money for more than just beans. A person who runs a cafe in Chicago said three costs had pushed prices up. These were cups, workers’ pay, and buying beans. Even if bean prices fall, other costs do not always fall with them.

If you are waiting for your usual cup to get cheaper, ask more than, “How much do beans cost now?” Also ask, “When does the bean price reach here?” A coffee price tag may have its own hidden clock, separate from the latest market news.

## In one line
Falling coffee bean prices may take at least nine months to affect US shop prices.

# Coffee Bean Prices Fall. Are Price Tags Still on a Journey?

“Beans have gotten cheaper!” At that news, your wallet pumps its fist. In your mind, the price of your usual cup has already come down, too. But the price tag in a shop may not change right away. When you see a price tag that makes you want to say, “Haven’t you heard the news?”, it seems there is a time lag.

The price measure reported by the International Coffee Organization fell 8.7% from the previous month. The reason, it said, was that more beans harvested in Brazil had entered the market, and a good supply was expected to continue.

The US Department of Agriculture said that earlier high prices came from several factors happening at once: bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam, fewer beans available for sale, and strong demand.

Meanwhile, US consumer price data showed that the price of coffee was 6.1% higher than in the same month a year earlier. It may leave you wondering, “Did prices go down or up?” But the data covers a different month from the bean price measure. And it does not show the price of a cup at a cafe. Hold on before putting the two figures in the ring.

So, how long does it take for the price of beans to reach a price tag?

According to estimates from market insiders and experts interviewed by Reuters, it takes at least about nine months for the price of raw beans to show up in US retail prices. The road to a price tag is quite a long journey.

The article says that companies in the US that roast coffee keep raw beans in stock. Roasting and packing the beans also take time. They also often negotiate prices with retailers on a regular basis. The price tag in a shop does not flash to a new price the moment the market moves.

However, the “about nine months” figure is an estimate based on interviews. It is not a rule that applies to every company, and it is not a promise that “prices will fall in nine months.” It is too soon to mark the date on your calendar.

And a cup at a cafe comes with costs besides the beans. One cafe operator in Chicago said that the cost of cups and labor, as well as the cost of buying beans, had been behind price increases. Even if bean prices fall, other costs do not always fall along with them.

If you are waiting for the price of your usual cup to come down, think not only, “How much do beans cost now?” but also, “When does the price of the beans reach here?” A coffee price tag may have an unseen clock of its own, separate from the latest news about the market.

## In one line
Falling coffee bean prices may take at least nine months to affect US retail prices.

# “Cockroach Milk”: Before You Get a Cup, Look at How It Stores Food

If you hear “cockroach milk,” the café in your mind shuts down. I understand. But let’s put the urgent meeting about drinking it on hold. The story is not its taste or how it feels to swallow. It is how baby cockroaches store food just for themselves.

The Ig Nobel Prize went to earlier research on crystals full of nutrients. This does not mean cockroach milk has finally appeared on the dinner table! No one drank it as part of the study. The study did not test it as food for people. Put the cup back on the shelf.

The study looked at a kind of cockroach that keeps its babies inside its body. Researchers took protein crystals with nutrients from the gut of the unborn young. You may think you are heading to the milk aisle. Instead, you see the food store inside a body.

The researchers used X-rays to study the shape of the protein inside the crystals. Fats stuck to the protein, and sugars stuck to it too. You may have expected a fancy latte. Instead, you got a map of molecules. Suddenly, we are in a science lab.

The paper gives a surprising estimate. The crystals have over three times as much energy as the same weight of milk. The milk came from several kinds of mammals.

“The final boss of nutrition?”

The marketing team may be ready to jump into action, but wait. The comparison was between “crystals” and “milk.” It does not mean that drinking them would make people three times as energetic. Take that number alone, and soon a science story can turn into a TV shopping show.

The more interesting idea is turning nutrients into crystals and storing them away. No fridge, no lunch box. If tiny crystals can store food, that is a clever way to save space.

The authors also say storing nutrients as crystals may help feed the young. But this role has not been confirmed. Next to “That makes sense!” there should be a sign saying “Still being studied.” The two should be shown together.

When you hear “packed with nutrition,” ask, “Compared with what?” and “For whom?” Behind the exciting number, you may find something else that is interesting.

Do not see this as a possible breakfast for people. See it as a way to bring nutrients to the young. They have not been born yet. You do not need to be brave enough to drink it. Today, bring your curiosity, not a cup. Look inside this little food store.

## In one line
Researchers studied protein crystals with nutrients in unborn cockroach babies, not cockroach milk for people. The crystals may help feed the babies, but this is not confirmed.

# If You Didn’t Write with AI, You Can’t Apply

What if a literary prize had a rule like this for entry? Not “You may use AI,” but “You must write with AI.” Wait, is that really required? I thought AI was a helper working behind the scenes. Now it is openly the ticket to enter.

The Prix Pascal was announced in France. It is for French stories that have not been published, written by a person and AI together. Using AI is not an extra benefit or a special case. If you have not used it, you cannot apply.

It may be too soon to say, “At last, we can compete to see how well AI can write.” What I want to know is not about the writers. It is about the people giving the prize. Why did they create a prize with this special rule for entry?

The people behind the prize say they want to ask other literary prizes a question. Those prizes are trying to decide what to do about writers using AI. They create one prize and ask the others, “So, what would you do?” You could call it a question shaped like a trophy.

Imagine you are reading a story late at night. The last line moves you. Then you hear, “Actually, I wrote it with AI.” Would a line that seemed beautiful suddenly feel far away? Or would you say, “I enjoyed it, so I have no complaint”? A special meeting to judge the story might start inside your mind.

Of course, the label “co-written with AI” does not mean the story is interesting. I would not want to read it just because of that, either. I want to know what kind of story it is and how it is written. Before the label, I want to see the first page.

But when I think about being the writer, things become much harder. I might ask AI to fix a phrase or help me think about what happens in the story. But how much can I use it and still proudly say, “I wrote this”? Where is the line between a helpful partner I can talk with and someone who writes with me?

So it would be a shame to make this prize only a simple question: “Is AI good or bad?” A prize that chooses stories also shows what the people choosing them value. The question of whether AI was used does not end the discussion. Instead, it becomes the starting point for reading. It seems writers are not the only people being tested at this new entrance. So, how will we read that book?

## In one line
France has announced a prize for unpublished French stories written by a person and AI. Its founders ask other prizes to think about AI, and readers to think about how AI changes reading.

# Bags Split the Job: Mini Bags Catch the Eye, Large Bags Carry the Load

In 2026 fashion, mini bags are having a big moment. Palm-sized clutches, small pouches, and eye-catching minaudières fill runways and fashion reports. Some are so small that you might ask, “Can you really fit anything in that?”

But mini bags are not taking over. They are not pushing large bags away. In 2026, the two sizes seem to have different jobs. One carries what we need. The other helps create the look.

ELLE included mini bags among its fall and winter 2026 style trends. Its examples included Khaite’s palm-sized evening clutch and Chanel’s novelty minaudière. They mostly hold the basics: a phone, wallet, keys, and lip products. They cannot compete with roomy bags for storage. Their job is visual. They add a special feeling. They say, “This is today’s mood.”

We see the season more clearly by looking at bags beside them.

Vogue also covered the 2026 season. It showed small pouches from Prada and Loewe. It also showed Celine’s Ultra Maxi and Altuzarra’s large shoulder bag. It showed roomy totes from Toteme and other brands, too.

This list matters. Large bags had not disappeared. Small and large bags appeared in the same season.

We are not seeing mini bags spread through the whole market. Instead, they are back in fashion reports and on certain runways. Even so, trends now look different. Bags no longer play a game with only one size on the throne. Large bags are the luggage crew. They carry what we need. Mini bags are the stage crew. They catch the eye and set the mood. In 2026, the runway proudly shows this split in their work.

## In one line

In 2026, large bags carry the load, while mini bags carry the mood.

But this is not a takeover, with mini bags pushing large bags out. In 2026, the two sizes seem to have different jobs. One carries what we need. The other helps create the look.

ELLE listed mini bags as one of the trends in fall and winter 2026 styling. Its examples included Khaite’s palm-sized evening clutch and Chanel’s novelty minaudière. They mainly hold the basics: a phone, wallet, keys, and lip products. They do not challenge roomy bags on storage. Their job is visual: adding a sense of occasion and saying, “This is today’s mood.”

The season’s picture becomes clearer when we look at what appeared beside them.

Vogue, also covering the 2026 season, showed not only small pouches from Prada and Loewe, but also Celine’s Ultra Maxi, Altuzarra’s large shoulder bag, and roomy totes from Toteme and other brands. This lineup matters: large bags had not vanished. Small and large bags were appearing in the same season.

What we see here is not mini bags spreading across the whole market, but their return in fashion coverage and on selected runways. Even so, the way trends look has changed. Bags are no longer in a game where one size alone sits on the throne. Large bags are the luggage crew, carrying what we need. Mini bags are the stage crew, drawing the eye and setting the mood. In 2026, the runway is proudly showing this division of labor.

## In one line

In 2026, large bags carry the load, while mini bags carry the mood.

# Could Musk’s “Good Idea” Slow Merger Talks?

“If the boss wants it, things move fast.” It is a familiar hope in meetings and business talks. But talks about joining Tesla and SpaceX may bring the opposite result. You think you have pressed the gas, but the brake lights come on. People are starting to worry about this kind of change.

Musk supported joining the two companies. He called it “a good idea.” But he says the choice should be left to special committees at both companies. Do not decide too soon. There are still steps between “he supports it” and “the merger is decided.”

According to Reuters, a person who knows about the talks is worried. They worry that Musk’s support and the public announcement of the talks may make shareholders look more closely. This could slow the talks. Support from a big name does not always make things move ahead quickly. This is not a report that the talks have already slowed.

The louder the support, the more attention it gets. When the star of the show steps into the spotlight, the audience watches more closely. Will people think, “Musk supports it, so we can relax,” or, “Wait, let’s check the details”? What matters is not how loud the support is. It is how others respond.

To begin, special committees at both companies are there to review the merger. Setting them up does not mean the merger is approved. In other words, they have only put out chairs for a meeting to review it. It is too early to set off the party poppers.

Shareholders must also follow certain steps to approve it. For some mergers and other matters, SpaceX’s articles of incorporation set rules. Holders of “Class B” shares must vote as a separate group and approve it. Other required approvals are needed too. Musk’s support is not a pass that opens every gate.

We do not know if talks will really be delayed this time. So watch not only, “Does Musk support it?” but also, “How will others react?” Will cheers help things move forward, or will closer checks make people drive carefully? A big name’s words can fire the starting gun or give people a reason to stop. Since someone has spoken in favor, we must watch others’ next moves in these talks.

## In one line
Musk called a Tesla-SpaceX merger “a good idea,” but it is still under review. A person who knows the talks worries Musk’s support and the public announcement may make shareholders look more closely and slow talks, but no delay has been reported.

# Is Your Video Putting on an Unwanted Show on the Train?

You get on the train and find a seat. At last, you can relax—or so you think. Then you hear sounds from a video somewhere: laughter, sound effects, and cheerful music in the background. You are quietly going home. But your ears have to log in to someone else’s video suggestions. You paid for a train ticket, but you don’t remember paying to see this show.

One smartphone makes the whole train carriage an audience. That’s a pretty bold show.

Here’s news about this kind of “sound no one asked for.” On October 19, 2026, the UK announced the start of a national campaign. It asks train passengers to use headphones.

But don’t quickly think, “In the UK, no headphones means you’re breaking the law!” No new rule bans all sound. The campaign points to current rail rules and asks people to think about others.

Current rail rules ban sounds from a device when they bother other people. They may cover sound from a phone speaker, too, if the situation fits the rules. There is an exception when the train company has given written permission. A song may sound like a masterpiece to you, but not to the person beside you.

If you break the rules, you could get a fine of up to £1,000. That’s enough to make you reach for your wallet before the volume button. But remember the words “up to” and “could.” It doesn’t mean everyone who plays sound on a speaker gets a £1,000 fine.

So the first step is a call to use headphones. People will see the message on posters and hear it in announcements at stations and on trains. The fine may be what people hear most, but let’s hear the campaign’s message, too.

Its name means something like, “Share the journey, not the noise.” Just because we’re in the same carriage doesn’t mean we’ve joined the fan club for the same video. The words draw that line simply.

This isn’t saying, “Don’t enjoy yourself.” It’s more like saying, “Choose who hears the sound.” You can enjoy videos and music. Just don’t make people around you sit in the audience without asking them. Headphones don’t take away your entertainment. They’re a small screen that keeps the fun in your own seat.

The next time you press play, take a breath. “Who am I sending this sound to?” We’re on the same train, going the same way. Still, the sound doesn’t have to ride into everyone else’s ears.

## In one line
The UK has started a national campaign asking train passengers to use headphones, not banning all sound. It asks people to enjoy videos and music without making other passengers listen.

Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.”

Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death.

“Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.”

The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.”

Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak.

“Go now, because I know you will come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.

He left for the city before daylight on day three.

The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.

The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.

Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.

By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him.

He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home.

But his friend would lose his life instead.

For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.

He managed one step, then took another.

At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death.

He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.

“Stop now! I’m back!”

His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.

“I almost left you to die,” he said softly.

“I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied.

They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.

The ruler kept his eyes on them.

Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.”

More softly, he then asked, “How can a man win such trust?”

For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

Silence followed. Then the guards seized the young shepherd, and the ruler sentenced him to death.

“Give me three days,” Melos said. “My sister is getting married. Let me see her wedding. I will return.”

The ruler smiled. “Your friend will stay here. If you are late, he dies instead.”

Melos turned to his friend, but before he could speak, his friend held out his hands for the chains.

“Go. I know you’ll come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laughter rose above the other voices. Melos listened closely. He wanted to remember exactly how it sounded.

Before dawn on the third day, he left for the city.

At the river, he stopped. The bridge was gone. Rain had turned the water brown and violent. He stepped back, ran, and threw himself into the flood.

The current pulled him under. He fought toward the light, caught a branch, and dragged himself onto the far bank.

Farther along, three men blocked the road. A knife flashed. Melos struck the man holding it with his walking stick and ran uphill, their shouts following him.

By afternoon, every step hurt. Blood stained his feet. He fell beside a rock and tried to rise, but his legs would not obey.

He could wait here. Someone might find him. He could go home.

His friend would die.

For one terrible moment, that seemed easier than getting up.

Then he remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend had trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water dripped from a crack in the rock. Melos drank, pushed himself onto his knees, and stood.

One step. Another.

At the city gates, the execution bell rang.

He ran toward the square. Above his friend, the sword was already raised.

“Stop! I am here!”

His friend turned. Melos fell against him.

“I nearly abandoned you,” he whispered.

“I nearly stopped believing,” his friend answered.

They held each other as the last sunlight touched the walls.

The ruler stared at them.

“Lower the sword,” he said at last. “Free them both.”

Then, more quietly, he asked, “How does a man earn such trust?”

For the first time, he waited for an answer instead of ordering one.

units.article_text:
Framton Nuttel felt nervous, even in this quiet sitting room. He kept turning his letter of introduction between his fingers. His doctor wanted him resting quietly in the country, not visiting strangers.

“My aunt will come downstairs in a minute,” said the fifteen-year-old sitting opposite him. “How well do you know her?”

“I don’t really know anything about her.”

The girl’s eyes turned towards the French window, open onto the lawn.

“Doesn’t that open window seem strange at this time in October?”

“Well, the weather’s still quite warm,” Framton answered.

“Her husband and two young brothers went shooting three years ago today. They went outside through that very window.”

For a moment she stopped speaking, and Framton waited.

“They never came back from the marsh, where the ground seemed firm. All three sank into deep mud with their little brown spaniel. Nobody ever found their bodies.”

Framton’s fingers stopped turning the letter.

“She expects them back and leaves it open until dark. Her husband wore a white waterproof coat over his shoulders. Her youngest brother sang, ‘Oh, brother, why are you jumping?’ He always sang that to annoy her.”

The girl swallowed hard.

“When it starts getting dark, I sometimes almost feel they really will—”

Then someone opened the door.

His host rushed in, saying how sorry she was.

“I hope you’ve enjoyed talking to my niece. Is the open window all right with you? My husband and brothers will soon return from shooting. They’ll get my carpets so dirty!”

Framton tried to find a safe subject and explained his doctor’s orders. He needed complete rest, without any excitement. She listened, but kept looking past him towards the lawn.

Suddenly, she looked happy.

“They’re finally back!”

The girl watched the window with her mouth slightly open. Framton turned, feeling cold inside.

Three men with guns were crossing the lawn as darkness came. One wore a white coat over his shoulders, and a tired brown spaniel followed them.

A young man’s voice called in the evening light.

“Oh, brother, why are you jumping?”

Framton took his hat and stick and ran through the hall. He rushed out of the gate, forcing a passing cyclist into the hedge.

The men entered through the open window.

“Who’s the man who just ran away?” the husband asked as he cleaned his muddy boots.

“Such a strange visitor!” she replied. “He looked like he’d seen a ghost.”

“The spaniel frightened him,” the girl said calmly. “He told me he was terribly afraid of dogs. Once, a pack chased him into a cemetery. He spent the night in an empty grave, with the dogs looking down at him.”

She looked over at the sleepy dog.

“He told me they took turns.”

Framton sat on his chair’s edge, turning his letter of introduction. His doctor suggested country air, but visiting strangers brought little peace.

“My aunt will join us soon,” said fifteen-year-old Vera. “How well do you know her?”

“I know very little,” Framton answered.

Vera looked at the wide-open window leading onto the lawn.

“Something terrible happened to her exactly three years ago today.”

The letter lay still in Framton’s hands.

“Her husband and two younger brothers left through that window. They went shooting, taking their small brown spaniel with them. They tried crossing wet ground, but it broke under them. All of them disappeared, and nobody ever found their bodies.”

“How awful,” said Framton quietly.

“She still believes they’ll return, so she waits until dark. That’s why she leaves the window open,” Vera said more quietly. “Her husband carried his white coat over his arm. Her youngest brother sang, ‘Bertie, why do you bound?’ He always sang that song to annoy her.”

Her eyes moved across the lawn, but nobody was there.

“On evenings like this, I sometimes think they might appear.”

Her aunt came in quickly before Framton could answer her.

“Has Vera been looking after you? I hope the open window doesn’t bother you. My husband and brothers are coming back from shooting soon. Their boots will be muddy, as usual!”

Framton went cold because she really did expect them back.

He talked about his health problems and avoided the window. But his hostess hardly listened, often looking past him towards the lawn.

Then a happy smile suddenly appeared on her face.

“Look, they’re finally home!”

Vera’s eyes opened wide as she looked outside in fear.

Framton looked behind him.

Three men crossed the lawn with guns as daylight faded. One carried a white coat, and a brown spaniel followed.

A young man’s voice reached them across the silent garden:

“Bertie, why do you bound?”

Framton struggled for breath as the dead approached the house.

He took his hat and stick and hurried outside. Moments later, he was racing down the drive.

The men came through the window, hungry and covered in mud.

“Who just left?” her husband asked.

“Such a strange man,” she replied. “He described his nervous problems, then ran off without warning.”

“The dog frightened him,” Vera said, sounding perfectly calm. “He told me dogs terrified him. A group chased him into an empty grave in India. He stayed there all night while they growled above him.”

Vera needed only seconds to invent a story people believed.

She looked out across the empty lawn.

“Sometimes, on evenings like this, I almost expect to see them.”

Before Framton could reply, her aunt hurried into the room.

“I hope Vera has kept you company! You don’t mind the open window? My husband and brothers will be back soon. They’ve been shooting. Their boots will be covered in mud, of course!”

Framton felt a chill. So she really was waiting.

He began describing his illness, trying to keep his eyes away from the window. His hostess listened with only half her attention. Again and again, she looked past him towards the lawn.

Then her face brightened.

“Here they are at last!”

Vera stared outside, her eyes wide with horror.

Framton turned.

Three figures were crossing the lawn in the fading light, carrying guns. A white coat hung over one man’s arm. A brown spaniel followed close behind.

Across the quiet garden came a young voice:

“Bertie, why do you bound?”

Framton could scarcely breathe. The dead were coming towards the house.

He grabbed his hat and stick and rushed out. Within seconds, he was running down the drive.
